$comment: Performance budgets, measured in CI on every push. See scripts/perf-budget.mjs.
These are ceilings, not targets. A number here should be comfortably above
today's measurement and comfortably below the point at which a phone on a
hotel wifi starts to suffer — a budget set to the current value flags every
commit and gets raised reflexively until it means nothing.
Raising one is a deliberate act with a reason attached, in the same commit
as whatever needed the room. That is the entire mechanism: not that the
numbers are perfect, but that growing past them has to be noticed.

bundles.name: app JavaScript (gzipped)
bundles.why: The one number a phone on a bad connection actually feels. Today ~140KB. Raised from 140KB, deliberately and with the reason attached: the ceiling had 0.2KB of headroom, which is a budget that fails the next commit whatever that commit is, and a number nobody can land under stops being a budget and becomes a coin toss. 148KB keeps roughly a second of 3G as the bound while leaving room to work in. It is not permission to grow: the next lane that needs more should be shrinking this rather than raising it again, and the Draft screen — 2,700 lines, the largest thing in here — is where that work is. Raised from 148KB by the lineup-legality and partial-market round (24 September 2026), by 0.6KB, for +157 bytes of its own: the Team card's empty-slot fill, the fill count on the bench line, and the completeness check the display ladder now runs before it prints a market number. That round had 66 bytes to work in. It moved the missing-markets sentence to the server to get there from +209, and stopped short of cutting unrelated screens owned by other lanes to find the rest; the Draft screen is still where the shrinking work is. That work landed on 24 September 2026: the Draft screen moved to its own lazily-loaded `draft-*.js` chunk (budgeted below) and Demo Mode stopped running the engines, which together took this from 148.1KB to ~124KB. The ceiling is left where it was so the gain is visible as headroom; lowering it is a separate, deliberate decision.

bundles.name: app CSS (gzipped)
bundles.why: Render-blocking, so it is worse per byte than the JavaScript. Today ~7.7KB.

bundles.name: HTML shell
bundles.why: The document itself. Today ~1.6KB; growth here usually means something got inlined that should not have been.

bundles.name: everything the browser must fetch to render (gzipped)
bundles.why: The total, so splitting one large file into three does not quietly pass three budgets. Demo Mode is the one thing left out, because it is genuinely not on the render path — and it has a ceiling of its own directly below, so the exclusion buys nobody any headroom.

bundles.name: Draft screen, fetched only while a draft is ahead (gzipped)
bundles.why: The Draft screen and the mock draft behind it. `App.tsx` reaches them only through `lazy()`, and draws the screen only while `draftVisible` holds (see `web/draftGate.ts`), so outside the few weeks before a draft no page load fetches this at all. Split out of the entry chunk on 24 September 2026, which took ~14KB off every page load; it is budgeted here rather than excluded, for the same reason Demo Mode is. Today ~20.0KB, with the two small chunks it used to share with Demo Mode now folded into it. Anything the Draft screen shares with another screen stays in the entry chunk, which is correct: it is the other screen's cost.

bundles.name: Demo Mode, fetched only when a scenario is opened (gzipped)
bundles.why: Demo Mode is a placeholder now: one in-season week served from captured responses (`core/demo/placeholder/`), with no engine behind it. Nothing on a page load can reach it — every path is a dynamic import behind Settings or an explicit ?demo= — so it is budgeted apart from the shell. Cut from ~164KB to ~26KB on 24 September 2026, when the requirement changed from a full rehearsal of every screen (twenty-odd scenarios run through the production draft, start/sit, waiver, trade, matchup and defence engines) to something representative plus a cheap place to demo one new feature. The ceiling came down with it, from 164.6KB, because the old number was raised five times for engines this chunk no longer carries, and a ceiling six times the measurement would let them creep back unnoticed. The captured JSON is most of this chunk (~23KB). A future feature demo belongs in `FEATURE_ROUTES` in `placeholder/runtime.ts`; if it needs an engine, that engine is its cost and this is where it shows.

$chunkOwnershipComment: Chunk ownership, enforced by the same `npm run perf:budget` as the bytes
above. The budgets measure how much a page load fetches; this measures what
is in it.
Rollup places a module reachable from the entry in the entry chunk, whatever
else also reaches it. So one render-path import into a module Demo Mode runs
for real moves that module, and the whole tree behind it, out of demo-*.js
and onto every page load.
That has happened twice, and both times a person found it rather than a
check: `core/dst/planner.ts`, pulled in for `weekRange` to print a heading
and bringing 25KB of defence model with it, and `core/sleeper/scoring.ts`,
pulled in for a roster's shape and bringing its scoring table. Neither failed
a size budget at the commit that caused it, and neither could have — the
ceilings above carry headroom on purpose, and a leak that fits inside the
headroom is green.
watch      — regions whose modules belong to Demo Mode or to an engine
unless this file says otherwise.
renderPath — the modules in those regions that a page load genuinely needs,
as the build actually places them.
Anything else from a watched region, found in a chunk that is not demo-*.js,
fails the check by name. Adding a line to renderPath is the same deliberate
act as raising a number above: in the same commit as whatever needed it, with
the reason in the commit message. Adding one to turn a red build green is how
this stops meaning anything — the usual answer is to split the leaf the render
path needs into its own module, which is exactly what core/dst/weeks.ts and
core/sleeper/rosterShape.ts are.
Measured from the build's own source maps, so it reports what the bundler did
rather than what the imports suggest it should have done. See
scripts/lib/chunkOwnership.mjs and tests/chunkOwnership.test.ts.
$apiComment: API budgets, measured by scripts/measure-api-budgets.ts against the demo
dataset and enforced by the same `npm run perf:budget` as the bundles.
Two numbers per endpoint, because an API read gets slow in two different
ways and page weight measures neither:
gzipBytes — what the phone downloads for one tap.
waves     — how many times the server had to wait for the database
before it could answer. Statements issued together share a
wave; a statement that had to wait for a previous one starts
a new one. On D1 a wave is a network round trip, so this is
the number latency multiplies, and it is invisible in every
The wave count is why this exists. `/api/players/:id/detail` reached
seventeen serialized statements — four of them re-reading the same player
row — to assemble a payload of under a kilobyte, and nothing in the
repository would have failed if it had reached thirty. Ceilings, not
targets, and raised deliberately with the reason in the commit, exactly

apis.name: player detail
apis.why: The most-opened read in the app: every expanded card on five screens. Today 0.47kB in 3 waves — one to find the player, one for everything that depends on nothing, one for everything that depends on that. Five waves is room for a fourth dependency layer to be added deliberately; it is not room for the chain to grow back.

apis.name: draft board
apis.why: The largest answer this API sends, and the one whose growth nobody was watching. It was 11kB gzipped over 125kB of JSON, mid-draft, on a phone; the two known Draft-side trims have since landed and it is 4.9kB over 32kB — the ranking rationale is computed on every board, drawn on none, and no longer travels to a client. See core/draft/boardWire.ts. The ceiling came down with the payload: a 14kB ceiling over a 5kB answer would let the whole explanation creep back without failing. 17 waves today.
